title: Morning
purpose: Delivers the story's resolution: Nastenka's letter confirming she will marry the returned lodger, and the Dreamer's choice to bless rather than blame her, fixing the book's final meaning.

points.text: The morning after the night's events brings rain, gloom and a feverish, weakened narrator, mirroring his inner state.
The servant Matrona delivers a letter whose handwriting the narrator instantly recognises as Nastenka's.
In the letter Nastenka begs forgiveness, admitting she deceived both the narrator and herself and that their brief union was a dream.
Nastenka says she still loves the narrator and wishes she could love both men, echoing her earlier wish that the narrator were her lodger.
She explains her heart returned to the lodger so quickly because it had always belonged to him.
Nastenka announces she will marry the returned lodger next week and asks the narrator to remain her friend and brother and to meet them both.
The narrator weeps over the letter, then Matrona's cheerful remark about clearing cobwebs for a wedding lands as bitter irony.
He has a vision of Matrona, the room and the house across the street aging and decaying, and sees himself unchanged and equally lonely fifteen years on.
He refuses to blame Nastenka or shadow her happiness with bitterness or guilt, wishing her clear skies and untroubled joy.
The story closes on the question of whether a single moment of pure happiness is enough to justify a whole lifetime — the narrator's implied yes.
